_doc: Phase G.5 (Growth) — TL;DR + Key Takeaways content per blog post. scripts/inject-article-tldr.mjs reads this file and stamps two sentinel-bracketed <aside> blocks into each article: a TL;DR within the first 800 chars of #post-body, and a Key Takeaways block before the article-foot CTA. AI search engines (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, Claude) lift these blocks nearly verbatim — keeping the language tight and operator-specific is the work. Slug must match a directory under blog/. ES counterparts go in article-content.es.json (translated, not regenerated, so the editorial voice carries). When an article is added to data/post-end-cta.json + data/library-tags.json + data/tool-knit.json, ALSO add a TL;DR + key_takeaways here.

_status.review_required: First-draft content, written from each article's H2 outline + first paragraph. Don should review for voice + accuracy before promoting.
_status.voice_check: Each TL;DR uses 3-5 imperative-or-indicative bullets, no hedging language. Key Takeaways use declarative one-liners — never starting with 'You should' or 'Always' (corporate-rubric register).

tldr: Wix is fine for first-day, placeholder, pop-up sites — but it hits walls fast for any restaurant past its first year.
Six places it breaks: closed-system menu, slow mobile, hostage reservations, template-good SEO, no real customization, exit costs.
The math: a custom site usually pays back in 12-18 months for any restaurant doing $40K+/month.
key_takeaways: Your menu inside Wix isn't crawlable as Restaurant schema — Google can't rank individual dishes.
Wix mobile speed scores typically land in the 40s-50s out of 100; that's the platform, not your settings.
If your reservation system isn't on Wix's partner list, you're stuck with what they offer.
Exit costs (export, redirect, recreate) are real and invisible until you try to leave.
Wix is the right call when the site is genuinely disposable — pop-ups, ghost kitchens, season tests.

tldr: $100 of DoorDash revenue typically becomes $40-50 in your account after commission, packaging, and prep time.
The honest question is whether the order would exist without DoorDash — for most operators, less than half do.
The 2026 recommendation depends on your volume, your prime cost, and whether your own ordering page actually works.
key_takeaways: Run the math on YOUR ticket, not the average — commission tier moves with volume.
Direct ordering through your own site keeps the full margin AND keeps the customer relationship.
The break-even on a delivery-only ghost kitchen is different from a dine-in restaurant testing delivery.
DoorDash is still the right answer when you have no time to run direct + your kitchen has spare capacity.
Save your DoorDash scenario in Margin Math and re-run it whenever your tier moves.

tldr: Most price-raise anxiety comes from running the math on the wrong number — total revenue instead of contribution margin.
A 4-7% across-the-board raise typically loses fewer than 2% of reservations when paired with menu re-staging.
The website moves matter as much as the price itself: better descriptions, photos on the top-margin items, and clean reservation flow.
key_takeaways: Charm pricing ($X.95) still works for casual; round pricing ($X) reads upscale — the choice depends on your room.
Raise the prices on items where the description is best, not where the margin is worst.
Re-photograph the items you raise — the perceived value moves more than the actual change.
Put the reservation CTA above the fold the same week you raise prices; the site has to feel current.
Save the price-raise scenario in Margin Math; re-run when food cost moves more than 1.5%.

tldr: Claim, verify, then complete every field — most restaurants leave 30%+ of the profile blank.
Categories matter more than anything else: pick the most specific primary category your restaurant qualifies for.
Photos and Posts both decay — without a 15-minute weekly habit, the profile stops working within a quarter.
key_takeaways: Primary category controls which queries Google shows you for — change it carefully.
Add at least 10 real photos at setup; aim for 30 within the first 90 days.
Respond to every review within 48 hours — Google reads response rate as an active-business signal.
Google Posts expire after 7 days; a quiet profile slips down the local-pack ranking.
The 15-minute weekly habit (1 photo, 1 post, all reviews replied) compounds harder than any one-time fix.

tldr: Reviews compound — a restaurant going from 50 to 200 reviews typically sees a 15-25% lift in pack-card click-through.
Five-piece system: a printed QR card, a check-message line, a follow-up text, a website CTA, and a manager who actually reads them.
Don't buy reviews, don't gate, don't filter — Google's spam detection has gotten dramatically better.
key_takeaways: The QR card on the check beats every other ask method 4-to-1 in field tests.
A short text-after-meal — "hope you enjoyed dinner; we read every review" — converts when sent within 12 hours.
Five-star reviews matter less than the 4-and-3 stars you respond well to (Google reads responsiveness).
Negative reviews aren't fatal; ignored negative reviews are.
The compounding window is 90 days — the system that's been running 90+ days outperforms the one that's been running 30.

tldr: Find a Table changed how Google handles restaurant queries — the booking happens in Google before the visitor ever reaches your site.
If your reservation system isn't on Find a Table, you're losing 8-15% of search-driven reservations to competitors who are.
Three concrete moves recover most of the lost flow without giving up your owned booking surface.
key_takeaways: OpenTable, Resy, Tock, and SevenRooms are all currently wired into Find a Table — pick one if you're on none.
Don't disable reservations in GBP — that costs you the call-and-walk-in queries too.
Add reservation schema to your site so Google can verify the integration is real.
Restaurant Audit's GBP section flags Find a Table eligibility as a separate score.
The wider pattern: every Google surface that takes the booking before your site does costs you the relationship — get the booking, then get the email.

tldr: Independent-restaurant custom-website pricing in 2026 ranges from $2,500 to $25,000+, with most landing $6,000-$12,000.
Four real options: DIY platform ($25-50/mo), template-driven studio ($2.5-6K), full custom ($6-20K), agency-of-record ($25K+).
What actually drives the price: menu complexity, reservation integration, ordering integration, and how many languages.
key_takeaways: Pure design polish doesn't move bookings — load speed, mobile UX, and SEO foundation do.
A real custom site usually pays back in 12-18 months at any volume above $40K/month.
Red flags on the cheap end: no contract, no Lighthouse score guarantee, no source-code handover.
Red flags on the expensive end: "discovery phases" before mockups, retainer for content updates you should do yourself.
Run Tech Stack Detector on your current site before any quote — the baseline matters.

tldr: Seven pages do almost all the work: home, menu, hours-and-location, reservations, story, contact, and one current promotion.
Pages you probably don't need: separate "events" page, blog, gallery (the site itself is the gallery).
Structure that earns its keep: every page answers a hungry-at-11pm question in under 3 taps.
key_takeaways: The home page exists to answer one question: "is this what I want tonight?"
The menu page must be HTML, not a PDF — PDFs are dead in mobile + AI search.
Reservations belong above the fold on every page, not buried in a contact form.
Story page is the second most important after menu — it's what guests share to convince a friend.
Delete the "events" page; weave events into the home page as a current-promotion strip.

tldr: The reservation funnel is the most honest marketing stat in restaurant ops — and most operators have never measured it.
Six leaks, in order: hours unclear, reservation-CTA buried, mobile slow, menu missing, photos cold, schema absent.
Fixing the first three leaks alone typically recovers 8-15% of lost bookings.
key_takeaways: Hours visible above the fold has the highest single-fix impact in field tests.
If reservations require more than two taps from any page, the funnel is leaking.
Mobile load above 3 seconds correlates with a 30%+ bounce on the reservation page.
Menu absent or PDF-only is the second-largest leak — Google can't help you rank without it.
Run Restaurant Audit, save the score, fix the top two flags, re-run in 30 days.

tldr: Five small website moves, none of which require a redesign, compound to roughly 1% margin recovery for a typical mid-volume restaurant.
Each move is independent — pick the one that's easiest in your context and ship it this week.
The compounding argument is honest math, not a marketing pitch: each percentage point is worth $X annual at your volume.
key_takeaways: Hours above the fold: +0.20% margin, 30 minutes of work.
One primary reservation CTA: +0.25%, replaces every other booking link.
Direct own-ordering link up top: +0.30%, beats every third-party platform on margin.
Better descriptions on top-margin items: +0.15%, requires Menu Copy Inspector.
Delete every stale promo and old PDF: +0.10%, the cleanup nobody schedules but everybody needs.

tldr: ChatGPT is genuinely good at first-draft body copy, alt-text, and structured FAQ generation for restaurant sites.
Where it gets you quietly wrong: room-specific details, hyperlocal language, the menu's actual voice.
The one-page briefing that fixes it: 12 prompts that pin the model to your restaurant's specifics, not the model's averages.
key_takeaways: AI-generated copy ranks fine for SEO; it just sounds generic, which kills bookings.
Feed the model your printed menu PDF, not just dish names — the descriptions carry the voice.
Have a human re-write every "approximately" / "roughly" / "various" — those are AI tells.
FAQ schema is one of the highest-leverage AI uses; let the model write 12 questions and prune to 6.
Run Menu Copy Inspector on the AI output before publishing; it catches the dead-language patterns.

tldr: If you have a Google Business Profile and you're satisfied with it doing all the work, the answer might genuinely be no.
Where GBP falls short: it can't carry your story, your real menu copy, or any direct-relationship channel.
The five-minute test that tells you whether you need one — and what it would actually cost if you do.
key_takeaways: GBP gives you discoverability and basic info; a website gives you the relationship.
Without a website, you're renting your audience from Google — fine until Google's algorithm changes.
The five-minute test: if every regular found you a different way, you don't need a site yet.
If you genuinely don't need one, do the 30-minute GBP audit and walk away.
When you do need one, a $2,500 template site is enough to start; full custom comes when the room demands it.

tldr: Most restaurant operators who ask for an app actually want one of five cheaper tools that already exist.
The install problem alone kills most app projects: regulars won’t download it, and one-time visitors won’t bother.
Two narrow situations make an app the right call: 5,000+ weekly app-relevant transactions, or a concept that genuinely requires app-level behavior.
key_takeaways: POS-native loyalty (Square, Toast) handles “I want a loyalty program” for $0 extra.
SMS opens at 90%+ vs push notifications at 5–15%; SMS is the better channel for “tell my regulars something.”
A mobile-excellent website plus a well-built Google Business Profile delivers “brand in their hand” without an install.
A progressive web app (saved to home screen) covers own-pocket ordering without an app store at all.
A POS-connected CRM gives you regulars data without owning custom code.

tldr: POS integration with a restaurant website is either real or theatrical: Toast and Square deliver the real version, Clover delivers the theatrical one.
Toast and Square both score 7 confident-yes marks out of 10 on the integration features that matter; Clover scores 1.
Clover wins on hardware variety; loses on every other feature that touches a website integration.
key_takeaways: Native online ordering eliminates the tablet-handoff middleman that Clover still leans on.
Square is the only POS with public, transparent pricing on its own site — that matters for trust at small-restaurant scale.
Toast is restaurant-specific from day one; Square retrofitted from retail; Clover was aimed at general SMB.
Contract flexibility (month-to-month, low switching cost) is a Square-only win at this scale.
Match the POS to your operating model, not the sales-rep pitch — kitchen-ticket pipeline matters more than brand fit.

tldr: Google’s AI Overview answered 13.14% of US desktop searches in March 2025 and is approaching one in five in 2026; restaurant queries trigger it more often.

Five paragraph-level moves get a restaurant cited: answer-first ≤45-word paragraphs under each H2, numbers in the lede sentence, predicate-shaped “X is Y” sentences with no hedge words, schema-anchored entity matches between prose and JSON-LD, and stable URLs once cited.
Citation is a different ranking axis than blue-link SEO — the page with the most backlinks doesn’t always get cited; the page with the cleanest extractable answer does.
key_takeaways: Strike these hedge tokens on the citation rewrite: approximately, usually, in some cases, most, often, typically, around, tend to, may, can.
The first paragraph below each H2 is the only one most AI extractors read — bury the answer in paragraph three and the page is invisible to the box.
The model cross-references your prose against your JSON-LD; mismatches between schema and prose drop citation odds, matches boost them.
Once cited, don’t move the page or paraphrase the paragraph — the crawler revisits cited URLs faster and a changed answer drops you from rotation.
If your traffic is mostly informational queries (hours, menu, reservations, dietary), pick citation; intent-rich (best Italian near me), keep ranking.

tldr: Google has indexed Instagram captions since 2024 and the in-app search bar handles 40% of restaurant discovery for guests under 35; almost no independent restaurant writes captions like it.

Five caption-level moves: the first nine words carry the keyword load, name the dish/cuisine/neighborhood, write for the search query not the photo, hashtags inside the sentence not stacked, fill the alt-text field every time.

Running the discipline on a real DMV account delivered 4.3x the saves and 2.1x the profile clicks vs the same restaurant’s old grid — saves and profile clicks are the only Instagram metrics that correlate with reservations.
key_takeaways: Instagram truncates the caption at ~125 characters on the feed — that’s nine to fifteen words; bury the dish name later and the post is invisible to search.
Three entities per caption is the discipline: the dish (specific, not category), the cuisine, and the neighborhood.
Stacked hashtags at the bottom were penalized in Instagram’s late-2024 update; two or three tags woven into the sentence outperform fifteen at the end.
Alt-text is searchable on both Instagram and Google; 90% of restaurant accounts skip the field and forfeit the surface free.
Likes don’t convert to bookings — saves and profile clicks do. Optimize captions for the metrics that actually move revenue.

tldr: The headline 30% commission is roughly identical across DoorDash, Uber Eats, and Grubhub; the second-layer fee stack opens a 2.5-point spread.
On the same $42 ticket, DoorDash Marketplace Plus keeps 18.4%, Grubhub Premium keeps 17.6%, Uber Eats Pro keeps 15.9%; direct keeps 28.9%.
Drop Grubhub first if you’re going to drop one — lowest volume, middle-pack kept-percent, highest rate of phantom-listing complaints in the DMV market.
key_takeaways: The platforms aren’t marketing — they’re a 30% margin tax for ~20% incremental revenue.
DoorDash adds sponsored-listing fees (~3% per promo order), Uber Eats adds Pro membership ($2.50/order), Grubhub charges a non-opt-in 1.8% communication fee per order.
At 12% operating margin, every third-party order has to drive 250% incremental revenue to break even on the platform spend as marketing — it almost never does.
Most operators are running ≥80% displaced relationship orders on the platform, not net-new discovery; the platform is a habit layer, not a discovery layer.
Convert third-party guests to direct on their second order through receipts and packaging inserts — that’s where the 30% commission actually pays back.

tldr: I delisted one of two DMV restaurants from DoorDash on April 7, 2026; daily revenue dropped 11% in week one and recovered to within 2.6% of baseline by week four.
Kept margin in dollars per day climbed 56% over baseline by week four because every recaptured order shifted from the 18.4% DoorDash channel to the 28.9% direct channel.
Total incremental kept margin: ~$4,000 across the month on a $58,000-gross restaurant. The platform was 90% displaced relationship orders, 10% net-new — not what I’d told myself.
key_takeaways: Customer complaints peaked at day 11 with 28 contact events; 68% of complainers converted to direct within two weeks at a 10% discount, 32% stopped ordering.
Packaging cost rose 18% in week three because the recaptured orders ran a larger average ticket ($46 vs $39) and more items per order.
Labor didn’t break — the line-cook schedule absorbed the channel shift by moving hours from late-evening DoorDash prep into mid-evening walk-in prep.
The Google review that went negative came down at day 21 when the customer accepted a $20 direct-channel credit — most delisting complaints are resolvable.
This is one restaurant in one market; the second restaurant I manage stays on the platform because the urban-density and Uber-flow dynamics there are genuinely discovery-driven.

tldr: Four loyalty models compete for an independent operator’s setup time: paper punch cards, integrated POS loyalty (Toast/Square), standalone platforms (Fivestars/Como), and CRM-direct (Mailchimp/Klaviyo + own checkout).
Paper punch cards return 75:1 on a 500-customer base; standalone platforms return 1.17:1; CRM-direct returns ~7x the punch card but only when the direct channel is already converting.
The loyalty conversation is downstream of the channel conversation — fix the channel first, layer the loyalty after, on the direct surface where margin can fund a real customer relationship.
key_takeaways: Standalone loyalty platforms (Fivestars, Como Sense) cost $165–$249/month and return ~$2,800/year — a 1.17:1 ratio that loses to the $10/year punch card on percentage terms.
POS-integrated loyalty (Toast Rewards, Square Loyalty) sits in the middle on ROI but the data is owned by your processor — it doesn’t come with you if you switch.

The CRM-direct path wins because it lets you segment: weekly regulars get tasting-menu invites with no discount, lapsed customers get a $15-off email at day 58, first-time direct buyers get a thank-you with a next-visit offer.
Don’t pay both a standalone platform and a POS-integrated loyalty — that’s a double-spend with overlapping returns.
If your channel mix is wrong (mostly third-party app orders, no direct flow), no loyalty layer fixes it; fix the channel first.

tldr: Four review archetypes need four response shapes: the glowing 5-star (short, warm, name a detail), the disappointed 3-star (acknowledge the specific issue, name the fix, invite back with a gesture), the angry 1-star (calm, factual, never match tone), and the legitimate-complaint 2-star (own it without ornament).
The future reader, not the reviewer, is your audience — the 3-star response is the most-read because that’s where undecided guests calibrate.
Never write “Thank you for your feedback,” “We strive to provide,” “We take this very seriously,” or “I’m sorry you feel that way” — corporate boilerplate signals not-from-an-owner.
key_takeaways: Sign the response with your first name and title — the signature tells future readers a human is on the other end.
Name the specific issue, the specific fix, and the specific make-good; vagueness reads as deflection.
Never match the angry reviewer’s tone — calmness in the response signals operational maturity to the next 1,000 readers.
AI Overviews now sometimes lift review responses into the cited paragraph alongside menu and About copy; corporate boilerplate makes you cite-able as corporate boilerplate.
The 1-star response stays under five lines — longer responses read as fighting the review instead of letting it be.

tldr: DC’s Initiative 82 phase-out makes the tipping-vs-service-charge question urgent; three models are now in play across the DMV: traditional tipping, 20% service charge, and hybrid (5% menu lift + optional tip).
Same $200 dinner check: server take-home varies $9, operator net varies $7, customer pays roughly the same all three ways but feels different about it.
I’d pick the 20% service charge if opening today — cleanest math for kitchen-retention, simplest compliance frame, and it forces operator honesty about what the meal actually costs.
key_takeaways: The service-charge restaurant draws 1.4% customer complaint rate vs 0.2% at the traditional-tipping restaurant in paired-restaurant data — real but manageable.
The hybrid model has the lowest complaint rate but the highest operator-time cost (roughly 2x the other two models, ongoing).
A clearly-posted distribution policy (server X%, kitchen Y%) cuts service-charge complaints from 1.4% to under 0.5%.
Migration windows are easiest at model-change moments — a renovation, a menu rewrite, a concept launch — rather than mid-stream.
If running hybrid and your average voluntary tip is below 4%, the model isn’t working — migrate to a clean service charge.

tldr: Four causes cover 100% of restaurant map-pack invisibility in the DMV market: unclaimed listing (40%), wrong primary category (30%), suspended listing (15%), duplicate listing (15%).
Three of the four fixes are same-day operator work; suspension and duplicate removal take 7–21 days but are tractable with documentation.
85% of restaurants find the fix within the first three diagnostic checks — the map pack is almost always a Google Business Profile problem, not a website problem.
key_takeaways: Primary category “Restaurant” is the worst possible choice — it puts you in competition with every other restaurant in your zip code; pick the narrowest cuisine-specific category instead.
Unclaimed listings rank lower than claimed ones by default and don’t show in the map pack at all post-Q1-2024.
A suspended listing reads as “Your Business Profile has been suspended” in the dashboard; reinstatement needs lease, business license, or utility-bill documentation.
Duplicate listings drop both pins from the map pack because Google can’t tell which is canonical — file the duplicate removal with proof.
If the 10-minute walk doesn’t resolve it, the residual ~5% of cases need NAP-consistency cleanup across the top 30 directories (60–90 minutes of work).

tldr: Sixty lines of JSON-LD that cover the six schema types Google reads first on a restaurant page — Restaurant, Menu, OpeningHoursSpecification, AggregateRating, Reservation, and FAQ.
Seven fields marked // EDIT (name, address parts, phone, hours, rating, menu items) are everything you have to change to make the example yours.
Three pre-publish checks: validator.schema.org for unknown properties, view-source for CMS-escaping bugs, and Google’s Rich Results test to confirm which surfaces your schema is eligible for.
key_takeaways: Schema is plumbing — it doesn’t move the needle on its own but it makes you eligible for surfaces (local-pack, AggregateRating stars, Reservation deep links, FAQ rich snippets, AI Overview citations) you weren’t eligible for before.
Once shipped, leave the schema alone — the crawler revisits stable JSON-LD more often and builds entity confidence over time.
Surface timing: local-pack and rating stars update in a week; Reservation deep links and FAQ snippets take 30+ days; AI Overview citations take up to 90.
When a fact changes, touch one field — new closing time, new menu item — and resist the urge to refactor.
Pair the schema with the citation-shaped writing from the AI Overviews piece for the highest-leverage single edit a restaurant site can ship in 2026.
